rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation removes `.float()` from anchor processing. Input Specification fixes dtype=torch.float32 for all tensors. When tensor is already float32, `.float()` is a no-op (returns same tensor unchanged). Therefore, removing `.float()` produces identical behavior for all float32 inputs regardless of numerical values.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation removes an explicit `.float()` type conversion call on the anchor tensor. However, the Input Specification fixes the dtype at torch.float32 for all input tensors. When a tensor is already float32, calling `.float()` on it is a no-op that returns the same tensor without any conversion or copy. Layer 2 testing confirmed bitwise equivalence across 112 rounds including random seeds and stress patterns (large magnitude, near-zero, sparse, boundary values). The mutation is semantically equivalent because the type conversion it removes would only have an effect on non-float32 inputs, which cannot exist under the fixed testing contract.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation only affects type conversion behavior, but input dtype is fixed at float32 per the Input Specification. To kill this mutant would require passing a non-float32 tensor (e.g., float64 or int32), which would violate the fixed specification. With float32 inputs, `.float()` is always a no-op, making the mutant equivalent.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing robustness, consider testing with multiple input dtypes (float16, float32, float64, int32) when the kernel supports type conversion. The current test specification locks dtype=float32, making type-conversion mutations undetectable. Add explicit dtype variation policies to the test contract, or mark type-conversion code as covered only when dtype diversity is tested.
